intro: “Smrt” (Death), the Adagio second movement of Janáček’s Piano Sonata 1. X. 1905, is a lament for a carpenter killed during the Brno university demonstrations. It opens with a broken phrase that returns many times, with more chords added around it, and grows from very soft to loud.

sections.label: A · Adagio phrase after a rest
sections.mNote: A small upward leap, then a fall back

sections.label: A · Opening phrase repeated, E♭ minor
sections.mNote: The repeat brings back the opening E♭-minor phrase.

sections.label: Dev · Chords under the broken phrase
sections.mNote: The left hand adds quick figures in reply.

sections.label: Dev · Left-hand repeated chords, accented melody
sections.mNote: Rapid repeated chords beneath a sharply accented melody.

sections.label: A′ · Opening phrase, fortissimo
sections.mNote: The opening melody returns over a busier left hand.

sections.label: Coda · Short closing phrases, soft pedal
sections.mNote: Short phrases thin out to a final E♭-minor chord.

cues.title: Opening phrases, Adagio
cues.text: Each short phrase begins after a rest. The right hand leaps from B♭ to E♭ and falls back, the left hand moves beneath it, and both hands then hold a chord. Janáček marks the movement Adagio, with the quaver at 56.
cues.evidence: Hudební matice score, plate H.M. 339, Štědroň reissue (1949), p. 9, opening of Smrt. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/6/62/IMSLP57304-PMLP117865-Jan%C3%A1%C4%8Dek_-_1.X.1905_%28%27Sonata%27%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Death of František Pavlík, Brno, 1905
cues.text: In October 1905 rival demonstrations over a proposed Czech university filled the streets of Brno, and troops were called in. The carpenter František Pavlík was fatally wounded. On 2 October, the day he died, Janáček began this sonata.
cues.evidence: Leoš Janáček Foundation, work history and chronology for 1. X. 1905. https://janacek-nadace.cz/dilo-leose-janacka/dila/1-x-1905/

cues.title: Repeat of the opening paragraph
cues.text: The first paragraph is repeated with the same small leap, the same pauses and the same brief forte. A second ending takes the piano into new chords.
cues.evidence: Hudební matice score, Štědroň reissue (1949), p. 9: opening repeat with first and second endings.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Tučková’s copy of the sonata
cues.text: At a rehearsal on the day of the 1906 première, Janáček burned the sonata’s third movement. He later threw the remaining manuscript into the Vltava. The pianist Ludmila Tučková kept her copy of the first two movements, which she brought forward in 1924, and they were then published.
cues.evidence: Leoš Janáček Foundation, work history: destruction of the finale, loss of the manuscript and Tučková’s surviving copy. https://janacek-nadace.cz/dilo-leose-janacka/dila/1-x-1905/

cues.title: Crescendo to fortissimo
cues.text: The melody keeps its clipped phrases. Below it the left hand plays quick figures, which spread into repeated chords. Successive crescendos take the piano from piano through forte to fortissimo.
cues.evidence: Hudební matice score, Štědroň reissue (1949), pp. 9–10, continuation after the second ending and successive written crescendos.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Left-hand chords under melodic fragments
cues.text: The left hand’s rapid chords now continue through the right hand’s rests. Above them, the melody is reduced to accented fragments, some of only two notes.
cues.evidence: Hudební matice score, Štědroň reissue (1949), pp. 10–11: continuous left-hand figures beneath rests and accented melodic fragments.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the opening phrase
cues.text: The opening phrase returns in E♭ minor, marked sforzando fortissimo. Its small leap is unchanged. The left hand plays continuous chords beneath it.
cues.evidence: Hudební matice score, Štědroň reissue (1949), p. 12, a tempo return marked sff, with continued left-hand chords.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final E♭-minor chord
cues.text: The returning phrases fall to a soft dynamic again. The last line reaches pianississimo, and for the final E♭-minor chord Janáček marks una corda, the piano’s soft pedal. The bass E♭ lies far below the closely packed notes above.
cues.evidence: Hudební matice score, Štědroň reissue (1949), p. 12, final two systems: ppp, una corda and final E♭-minor chord.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: First ending and repeat
transitions.from: A · Adagio phrase after a rest
transitions.to: A · Opening phrase repeated, E♭ minor
transitions.how: The first ending thins to a held chord under the soft pedal. At the repeat the opening E♭-minor bass returns, with the small upward leap in the right hand and the short rest before the phrase.
transitions.evidence: Hudební matice score, Štědroň reissue (1949), p. 9: first ending, una corda, repeat sign and opening phrase.

transitions.title: The second ending and left-hand figures
transitions.from: A · Opening phrase repeated, E♭ minor
transitions.to: Dev · Chords under the broken phrase
transitions.how: The second ending takes the piano past the repeat. Held bass notes support the clipped melody. The left hand then begins quick chord figures of its own between the melody’s phrases. The phrases still begin after rests, and the accompaniment fills more and more of the gaps between them.
transitions.evidence: Hudební matice score, Štědroň reissue (1949), pp. 9–10: second ending and the development of rapid left-hand figures.

transitions.title: Return of the opening melody
transitions.from: Dev · Left-hand repeated chords, accented melody
transitions.how: A ritenuto slows the rapid left-hand chords. At a tempo the opening melody returns over an E♭-minor bass, marked sff. The left hand continues the moving chords of the middle section beneath it.
transitions.evidence: Hudební matice score, Štědroň reissue (1949), p. 12: ritenuto followed by the a tempo return.

transitions.title: Closing bars in E♭ minor
transitions.to: Coda · Short closing phrases, soft pedal
transitions.how: The right hand repeats the short falling phrases, and the left hand continues its quieter chords. Janáček brought the final line down to ppp and then wrote una corda over the last E♭-minor chord. The bass ends on a low E♭.
transitions.evidence: Hudební matice score, Štědroň reissue (1949), p. 12, closing systems.

composer.epithet: Composer who wrote down the voices of strangers in Brno and wrote operas known for their recognisable characters.
facts: Chorister in Old Brno; organ studies in Prague; conservatories in Leipzig and Vienna
Founded the Organ School in 1881; directed it until 1919
Nine operas, two string quartets, Sinfonietta, Glagolitic Mass, piano music and folk-song collections
composer.background:
In August 1865, Janáček’s mother took her eleven-year-old son to Brno and left him at the Augustinian monastery. His father, a schoolmaster in Hukvaldy, was ill, and the family needed the scholarship. Nearly sixty years later, in his autobiographical sketch of 1924, Janáček recalled “a hard bed, harder bread. No caresses.” The monastery’s choirmaster, Pavel Křížkovský, taught him music. The boy sang at services, went to concerts and the theatre, and learned the profession that kept him in Brno for the rest of his life.

He trained as a teacher, studied at the Prague Organ School, and attended the conservatories in Leipzig and Vienna. In Prague he also formed a lasting friendship with Dvořák. Back in Brno he taught, conducted the Beseda choir and organised concerts; in 1881 he founded the Organ School, which he directed until 1919. His programmes included Beethoven’s Missa solemnis and Dvořák’s Stabat mater.
